evidence.claim: At Millwood, Nathaniel Burwell financed a mill whose construction Daniel Morgan managed about 1785.
evidence.quote: It was built about 1785 by Gen. Daniel Morgan and Lt. Col. Nathaniel Burwell, who both served in the American Revolution. Burwell was the project's financier and Morgan managed the construction.

evidence.claim: The mill worked until the 1950s, then passed to the Clarke County Historical Association in 1964.

evidence.claim: The association completed restoration in 1970 and operates it as a museum.

evidence.claim: Millwood lies southeast of Boyce, where the railway crossed the Winchester and Berry’s Ferry Turnpike.
evidence.quote: The town is situated at the crossing of the Norfolk & Western Railway and the Winchester and Berry's Ferry Turnpike about 2 miles (3 km) northwest of Millwood

evidence.claim: Paris stands at the eastern base of Ashby Gap, and Blue Ridge Mountain Road provides the mountain connection from the gap.
evidence.quote: Located in Virginia's hunt country, it was established in a strategic spot at the eastern base of Ashby Gap along U.S. Routes 17 and 50.

evidence.claim: Blue Ridge Mountain Road provides the mountain connection from the gap

evidence.claim: A stone in the mill wall carries the overseer’s initials and the date 1782.
evidence.quote: The project overseer was L.H. Mongrul, whose initials and the date 1782 are carved in a stone in the mill's wall.

evidence.claim: The mill’s construction is dated about 1785, with Nathaniel Burwell financing the project and Daniel Morgan managing it.
evidence.quote: It was built about 1785 by Gen. Daniel Morgan and Lt. Col. Nathaniel Burwell, who both served in the American Revolution. Burwell was the project's financier and Morgan managed the construction.

evidence.claim: Stone lower levels support a frame upper story and attic added around 1876.
evidence.quote: It consists of a down slope basement and first level of stone topped by a frame second story and attic addition, added around 1876.

evidence.claim: After milling ended in the 1950s, restoration made the building a museum.
evidence.quote: The mill operated until the 1950s. In 1964 it was donated to the Clarke County Historical Association, which finished restoration in 1970 and operates the mill as a museum.

evidence.claim: Its water wheel is a rebuilt one made of Peruvian mahogany.
evidence.quote: It features a rebuilt water wheel of Peruvian mahogany.

evidence.claim: The Clarke County Historical Association received it in 1964 and completed its restoration six years later, in 1970.
evidence.quote: In 1964 it was donated to the Clarke County Historical Association, which finished restoration in 1970

evidence.claim: The mill wall bears L.H. Mongrul’s initials and the date 1782.

evidence.claim: Blue Ridge Mountain Road gives access to Paris Mountain from Ashby Gap.
evidence.quote: The peak is accessible by Blue Ridge Mountain Road from the gap.

evidence.claim: Paris Mountain rises to 1,926 feet just north of the gap. Its summit is the highest point in both Clarke and Loudoun counties.
evidence.quote: The 1,926 feet (587 m) peak, which is located just north of Ashby's Gap and the town of Paris, for which it is named, represents the highest elevation in both counties.

evidence.claim: The Appalachian Trail crosses the peak’s western slope.
evidence.quote: The Appalachian Trail crosses the western slope of the peak.

evidence.claim: SR 601, also called Blue Ridge Mountain Road, is the approach to the Mount Weather Emergency Operations Center.
evidence.quote: access to the operations center is available via State Route 601 (also called Blue Ridge Mountain Road)

evidence.claim: The site began as a weather station in the late 1800s; its research observatory operated from 1904 to 1914.
evidence.quote: The site was opened as a weather station in the late 1800s. William Jackson Humphreys was selected as the supervising director for the Mount Weather Research Observatory, which was operational from 1904 to 1914.

evidence.claim: An underground facility was completed in 1959, and FEMA established surface training facilities in 1979.
evidence.quote: The underground facility within Mount Weather, designated "Area B", was completed in 1959. FEMA established training facilities on the mountain's surface ("Area A") in 1979.

evidence.claim: The bronze plaque on White Post’s marker records a tradition: George Washington placed the original post to direct travelers to Lord Fairfax’s residence.
evidence.quote: According to a tradition currently inscribed on a bronze plaque affixed to the post, then Col. George Washington set the original post to guide travelers to Lord Fairfax's residence.

evidence.claim: Fairfax employed the young Washington as a surveyor on his extensive landholdings.
evidence.quote: Fairfax employed a young George Washington on his extensive land holdings as a surveyor.

evidence.claim: His seat, Greenway Court, lies south of the village.
evidence.quote: south of the village of White Post.

evidence.claim: The original house was pulled down after its roof collapsed in 1834.
evidence.quote: Abandoned, the roof of the main house at Greenway Court collapsed in 1834, after which the structure was pulled down.

evidence.claim: The surviving land office is a limestone building from about 1762.
evidence.quote: The main historic structure surviving from the period of the Fairfax residency is the Land Office, a c. 1762 single-story gable-roofed limestone structure

evidence.claim: The crossroads itself joins White Post Road and Berrys Ferry Road off US 340. Greenway Court’s private drive lies on White Post Road, south of the village.
evidence.quote: White Post is located at the crossroads of White Post Road and Berrys Ferry Road off Lord Fairfax Highway (U.S. Route 340).

evidence.claim: Greenway Court’s private drive lies on White Post Road, south of the village.
evidence.quote: Greenway Court is located down a long private drive on the west side of White Post Road, south of the village of White Post.

evidence.claim: The gable-roofed building measures approximately 45 by 60 feet.
evidence.quote: The mill is a two-story structure with gable roof measuring approximately 45 feet by 60 feet.

flags: PARTIAL OVERVIEW: the cached List of Virginia Byways has no route table. No cache text establishes which Clarke roads have byway designation, their designation dates or an end-to-end route. General program purpose is supported; specific designation and designating-body rationale remain unverified.
Dropped unsupported current claims that Howellsville Road follows the Shenandoah and SR 601 runs atop the ridge from Snickers Gap to Ashby Gap. Material is context, not evidence.

Moment order follows the supplied strip's Boyce/Millwood, Paris/mountain, Greenway Court/White Post progression. This is a network, not a verified continuous itinerary; no turn-by-turn links asserted.
The 1782 mill-wall inscription and approximate 1785 construction date are both retained without an invented reconciliation.

White Post gives Fairfax settlement in the 1730s; Greenway Court gives estate layout in 1747. The disputed settlement date is omitted. Washington's post story remains a plaque tradition, not established fact.

Current Coolidge summer White House claim has secondary cache support but no underlying historical source; omitted pending corroboration. No public access to Mount Weather or Greenway Court is established.
All cache sources are secondary. Overview stays short because the drive character and modern road history are incompletely supported.
